newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak cbank sees no need to react to CZK fall.
newsitem.headline: Slovak cbank sees no need to react to CZK fall.

text.p: The National Bank of Slovakia (NBS) said on Tuesday it saw no need for any measures regarding the Slovak crown in reaction to the recent decline of the Czech crown.
"I would not call the Czech crown's decline radical and certainly not so significant as to require any NBS action to react to its fall," NBS vice-governor Marian Jusko told Reuters.
He added the current Slovak crown rate was "relatively" stable and could be maintained at least for the shorter term.

"We cannot say whether the central bank is satisfied or not with the movement of the Slovak crown, but we consider its rate relatively stable and certainly maintainable for at least the short term," Jusko said.
He declined to say how long the NBS saw the current crown rate as sustainable.

The Czech crown and its Slovak counterpart have been under speculative pressure initiated by foreign banks last week which prompted the Czech National Bank to intervene in the market to prop up its currency.
The CNB on Monday abolished the fluctuation band of plus/minus 7.5 percent within which it used to fix the crown.
Jusko said the Czech crown's decline was no threat to mutual Slovak-Czech trade. "The Czech crown's fall is not significant enough to threaten our mutual trade."
The Czech and Slovak economies remain closely linked even after the two countries split into separate states in 1993.
The Czech Republic is Slovakia's largest trading partner taking 27.9 percent of its exports in the first four months of 1997 and accounting for 23.2 percent of Slovakia's imports.
Bratislava's trade deficit with Prague totalled 1.998 billion crowns in the January-April period this year.
Local analysts said Slovakia would have to follow if the Czechs devalued their currency by more than 10 percent, pointing mainly to their close trade relations.
The Slovak central bank has so far resolutely rejected calls for devaluation of the currency.
The Slovak crown followed the Czech crown decline on Tuesday losing some five percent against its mark/dollar basket parity.
Local crown dealers said the fall hardly reflected the currency's real price since banks were trading only limited volumes due to low liqudity both on the forex and money markets.
